CausalChain: Fasting -> Metabolic stress -> Activation of AMPK -> Downregulation of glycolytic enzymes (HK2, PFKFB3, PKM2) -> Shift from aerobic glycolysis to OXPHOS -> Reduced lactate production and extracellular acidification -> Alleviation of tumor-induced immunosuppression -> Enhanced efficacy of PD-1/PD-L1 blockade
Hypothesis: Fasting induces metabolic stress in HCC cells that activates AMPK, leading to the downregulation of critical glycolytic enzymes (HK2, PFKFB3, PKM2) and a metabolic shift from the Warburg phenotype to oxidative phosphorylation. This shift reduces lactate production and extracellular acidification, thereby mitigating lactate-mediated immunosuppression within the tumor microenvironment. By integrating state-of-the-art techniques such as dynamic metabolic flux analysis, real-time molecular imaging, and single-cell sequencing, we propose to validate this cascade and demonstrate that the resulting microenvironmental changes synergistically augment the efficacy of PD-1/PD-L1 immune checkpoint blockade in HCC.
Abstract: This study proposes that fasting-induced metabolic stress in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) activates AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), which in turn downregulates key glycolytic enzymes (HK2, PFKFB3, and PKM2). This downregulation shifts tumor energetics from aerobic glycolysis to oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), leading to reduced lactate production and a consequent decline in extracellular acidification. The resulting decrease in lactate-mediated immunosuppression is hypothesized to sensitize tumors to PD-1/PD-L1 immune checkpoint therapies. Leveraging advanced technologies—including real-time metabolic flux analysis, molecular imaging, and single-cell sequencing—our approach seeks to precisely quantify each step of this cascade, thereby validating and potentially enhancing the efficacy of combined metabolic and immunotherapeutic interventions in HCC.
Orignal_vs_New: The revised hypothesis retains the core elements of the original causal chain—fasting leading to metabolic stress, AMPK activation, downregulation of glycolytic enzymes, a metabolic shift towards OXPHOS, reduced lactate production, and consequent alleviation of tumor-induced immunosuppression that enhances PD-1/PD-L1 therapy. However, it explicitly incorporates contemporary technological capabilities (e.g., real-time metabolic flux analysis, molecular imaging, and single-cell sequencing) to enhance the practical implementability and quantification of each causal step. This modification directly addresses the review comments by providing measurable endpoints and clarifying the mechanistic link between the metabolic reprogramming and the improved immune response, while also acknowledging potential compensatory metabolic pathways and systemic effects that could influence therapeutic outcomes.
